Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic forecast errors and derive correction rules.

## Example 1: Date 2025-06-02
- History: Price range ~70.41 to 73.41, generally stable around 71-72
- Sentiment: Varied from 0.00 to 1.00, mostly 0.67
- Model forecasts: Start at 71.02, gradually increasing to ~75.25 by day 30
- True outcomes: Start at 70.91, gradually increasing but model is consistently higher

Looking at the deviation:
- Day 1: Model 71.02 vs True 70.91 (overshot by +0.11)
- Day 5: Model 73.71 vs True 73.50 (overshot by +0.21)
- Day 10: Model 76.51 vs True 75.94 (overshot by +0.57)
- Day 15: Model 74.92 vs True 73.27 (overshot by +1.65)
- Day 20: Model 71.20 vs True 68.97 (overshot by +2.23)
- Day 25: Model 74.95 vs True 71.20 (overshot by +3.75)

The model consistently overforecasts prices, especially as we look further into the horizon. The gap widens significantly by day 25-30.

## Example 2: Date 2025-06-03
This is very similar to Example 1, just the next day. The pattern is the same - model forecasts are consistently above true outcomes.

## Example 3: Date 2025-05-30
This also shows the same pattern of model forecasts being slightly higher than true outcomes, with the gap widening toward the 30-day horizon.


I notice a consistent pattern of model overforecasting that becomes more pronounced as we look further into the future. The sentiment seems to play a complex role, with initial variations masking a underlying tendency to predict prices higher than actual outcomes.

The deviations appear to increase with time, suggesting the model struggles with long-term price accuracy. Sentiment fluctuations from 0.00 to 1.00 don't fundamentally alter the core forecast bias of overshooting current price levels.
